name: Grangemouth
title: Grangemouth UTM: Gauging for Feeder Ships and Product Tankers
description: Thickness gauging at Grangemouth for container feeders, product and chemical tankers and gas carriers: hull, ballast tank, deck and piping UTM.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement at Grangemouth on the Upper Forth
intro: Grangemouth sits at the inland end of the Firth of Forth, upstream of the three Forth bridges, and combines Scotland's largest container port with a petrochemical complex. Feeder container ships run short loops to the continental hubs, and tankers and gas carriers serve the industrial site. Calls are often brief, so gauging here is usually targeted and planned well ahead. Atlantis sends its technicians from India for each job, boarding at the berth or meeting the ship again when she moves on to a docking.

highlights.p: Container feeders on fixed weekly loops rarely stay long, so the gauging is split across calls. Deck, hatch coaming and accessible ballast tank readings taken on successive visits build up a full picture of the hull without delaying the ship or her next berth slot.

Product and chemical tankers call for the fuel import terminal and the chemical plants beside it. Cargo-area work needs gas-free tanks, so at the berth we concentrate on ballast tanks, deck structure and the piping that sits outside the cargo system.

highlights.h: Bridges, a buoyed channel and a lock
highlights.p: The approach runs up the Forth beneath the rail and road bridges and along a marked channel through the shallower inner Firth, and the docks are reached through a sea lock. Lock times decide when the team can board and how long the ship stays put.

port.h: Grangemouth: containers and petrochemicals on the upper Forth
p: Grangemouth lies on the south shore of the upper Firth of Forth where the River Carron meets the estuary, close to Falkirk and well inland from the open sea. Every ship bound for the port passes beneath the Forth Bridge, the Forth Road Bridge and the Queensferry Crossing before continuing up a buoyed channel through the shallower inner Firth, and the port is run by Forth Ports as its main container terminal in Scotland. Most commercial berths are inside enclosed docks entered through a sea lock, which keeps the water level steady once a ship is inside, while tankers serving the petrochemical complex use jetties on the river frontage. Pilotage is compulsory for the passage up the Firth, and the timing of each arrival depends on the tide, the lock programme and other traffic in the channel.

The container trade is a feeder business. Small and mid-sized container ships shuttle between Grangemouth and the deep-sea hubs on the continent, carrying Scottish exports such as whisky and food products out and consumer goods and raw materials in, often on weekly rotations with tight berth slots. Alongside them, the industrial complex has long been the port's other pillar. Petroineos stopped processing crude oil at the Grangemouth refinery in April 2025 and turned the site into an import terminal for transport fuels, which means the fuels the plant once made for itself now arrive by sea in product tankers. The chemical plants nearby have been served by gas carriers and chemical tankers, and bulk and general cargo ships use the docks as well, so the port sees a wider range of hull types than its container profile suggests.

The upper Forth is sheltered compared with the open coast, so weather rarely stops work on a ship alongside, though strong winds can delay lock operations and the passage under the bridges. More often the constraint is time. A feeder may be in the docks for less than a day, and a tanker at a terminal jetty works to the terminal's rules on equipment, access and permitted work. For gauging this means splitting scopes, preparing tanks before arrival and choosing the right moment, such as a ship waiting for the lock, a repair spell in the docks, or the days before a docking elsewhere. Fog occasionally settles over the inner Firth in still winter weather and slows traffic, and the agent's view of the lock programme is the best guide to how long a ship will really be available to the team.

facilities.h: Where gauging fits in at Grangemouth
p: Inside the enclosed docks, ships lie at quays with road access, so the team can bring gauges, lighting and ventilation equipment to the gangway without fuss. On a feeder container ship the realistic scope during a call is deck plating, hatch coamings and covers, deck fittings and their foundations, and ballast tanks the crew have opened and ventilated before arrival. General cargo and bulk ships discharging over several days allow hold gauging as each hold is emptied. Engine-room piping, including sea-water cooling and fuel lines, can usually be measured during any call because it does not depend on cargo operations.

Tankers at the terminal jetties are a different matter. Cargo tanks cannot be entered until they have been gas-freed, and terminals restrict what equipment comes aboard, so cargo-area gauging on a product or chemical tanker is normally planned for a lay-by period, a repair spell or the docking itself. When a docking is due, ships from Grangemouth either drop down the Firth to the Babcock yard at Rosyth or sail for yards in Poland, the Netherlands or elsewhere in northern Europe, so a Grangemouth call is often the place to take pre-docking readings.
list: Container berths in the enclosed docks — deck, hatch cover, coaming and ballast tank gauging on feeders during a call or across several calls.
General cargo and bulk berths — hold and tank gauging as discharge empties each space.
Lock and lay-by berths — longer scopes on ships waiting for a slot or held in port between voyages.
Terminal jetties on the river — piping and deck checks within terminal rules; cargo tanks only once gas-freed.
Rosyth drydocks down the Firth — full renewal-survey scopes when a ship moves on for docking.

context.h: Port state control, tanker vetting and emissions rules
p: Port state control at Grangemouth is carried out by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency within the Paris MoU, and the UK, outside the EU, runs its own ship recycling regime in place of the EU regulation. Tankers and gas carriers also face the oil companies' and terminals' vetting systems, and for a chemical or product tanker a SIRE inspection report that mentions wasted deck lines, corroded vent heads or doubtful ballast tank coating will raise questions at the next fixture. Current readings on deck piping, vent and air pipes and ballast tank structure are the simplest way to answer those questions with figures rather than assurances.

The feeder trade between Grangemouth and continental hubs sits squarely inside European emissions rules as well. Half of the emissions on each voyage between Grangemouth and an EU port fall under the EU Emissions Trading System, and FuelEU Maritime counts the energy used on those voyages in the same proportion, which keeps feeder operators focused on hull condition and fuel consumption. Ships on these rotations call at EU ports every week, so they carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials for EU purposes as a matter of course. The refinery's switch to an import terminal has not removed tanker calls; it has changed what they carry and where it comes from.

jobs.h: Thickness measurement work typical of Grangemouth
jobs.p: Grangemouth jobs are shaped by short calls. For feeder operators we often plan gauging across a series of visits, so that the deck and accessible ballast tanks are covered piece by piece and the full report is ready before the renewal survey. Tanker work at the berth concentrates on what can be reached without gas-freeing cargo tanks: deck structure, vent and air pipes, ballast tanks and engine-room piping. Longer stays come when a ship is held between charters or is waiting for a repair, and those are the windows for hold and cargo-area gauging. Each job is fixed with the superintendent, the ship's agent and, where relevant, the terminal before the team travels from India.
list: Staged gauging on a container feeder over several rotations, covering deck, coamings and ballast tanks ahead of her renewal survey.
Deck piping, vent head and air pipe UT on a product tanker at the terminal, answering findings from a vetting inspection.
Ballast tank and double-bottom gauging on a chemical tanker during a lay-by period between charters.
Hold and hopper tank gauging on a bulk carrier discharging in the enclosed docks.
Pre-docking steel estimate for a feeder ship before she leaves for a yard in northern Europe.

logistics: Edinburgh Airport is the nearest international airport, and Glasgow Airport is an alternative; both are within driving distance of Grangemouth. The team needs UK visitor visas, so the expected call date is requested early, and for feeder ships on fixed rotations the visit can be planned weeks ahead. The ship's agent arranges port passes through the ISPS-controlled gates, and work on a tanker at a terminal jetty also needs the terminal's permission and any induction it requires.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a container feeder in the time she spends at Grangemouth?
faqs.a: Partly, and that is usually enough. In a single call we can cover deck plating, hatch coamings and covers, engine-room piping and one or two ballast tanks the crew have opened beforehand. For a full programme we split the work over consecutive calls on the ship's rotation, recording each set of readings against the class sketches so the final report is complete when the survey comes due.

faqs.q: Do you gauge cargo tanks on tankers at the Grangemouth jetties?
faqs.a: Not while the ship is working cargo or the tanks hold vapour. Cargo tank gauging needs the tanks cleaned, gas-freed and certified for entry, which normally happens at a lay-by berth, during repairs or in dock. At the jetty we can take readings on deck structure, vent and air pipes and ballast tanks, provided the terminal accepts the equipment and the work.

faqs.q: Has the refinery closure changed what ships call at Grangemouth?
faqs.a: It has changed the tanker traffic rather than ended it. Since crude processing stopped in 2025 the site has worked as an import terminal for transport fuels, so product tankers deliver finished fuels by sea. Container, bulk and general cargo traffic through the docks carries on as before, and the neighbouring chemical plants have their own separate gas carrier and chemical tanker traffic.

faqs.q: Where do ships from Grangemouth go for drydocking?
faqs.a: Some use the Babcock yard at Rosyth, a short distance down the Firth, which takes commercial dockings alongside its naval work. Many feeder and tanker operators dock at yards in northern Europe instead. Either way, readings taken in Grangemouth give the yard a steel estimate before the ship arrives, which helps plan the dock period and order material in good time.
